name: Hungarian National Gallery
description: The country's largest public collection of Hungarian fine art, displayed in the royal palace on Buda Castle hill. Founded in 1957 and installed in the castle in 1975, it holds medieval wooden altars, Gothic panel paintings and works by Munkácsy and Csontváry, and the palace also contains the Habsburg Palatinal Crypt.

children.text: The Hungarian National Gallery is the largest public collection documenting Hungarian fine art. It was established to display Hungarian art and first opened on 5 October 1957 in the building that had formerly housed the Supreme Court. In 1959 the government designated Buda Palace as its future home, and in 1975 the gallery moved into Buildings B, C and D of the palace, with its exhibitions opening in provisional form that October. Building A of the castle was acquired in 2005, adding exhibition space. At its founding the collection already held about 6,000 paintings, 2,100 sculptures, 3,100 medals, 11,000 drawings and 5,000 prints.

The setting is as much a part of the visit as the art. The palace on this site dates back to the 14th century, with building work under Louis the Great, Sigismund and Matthias Corvinus. It was badly damaged during the Ottoman occupation from 1541 and the Battle of Buda in 1686, and Baroque rebuilding began in 1749 under Maria Theresa. Miklós Ybl and Alajos Hauszmann later enlarged it, and the palace was inaugurated in 1912. The siege of Budapest reduced it to ruins in 1944–45; it was rebuilt by 1966, with Lajos Hidasi's modernist dome dating from 1961, and the interiors were completed only in the 1980s.

Inside, the collection runs from the Middle Ages to the 20th century. It includes 15th-century wooden altars, Master MS's The Visitation from Selmecbánya and works by Károly Markó the Elder, Pál Szinyei Merse, József Rippl-Rónai and Tivadar Kosztka Csontváry. The museum's catalogue lists a version of Mihály Munkácsy's Christ before Pilate, dated 1881. The gallery's permanent displays were assembled step by step: medieval panel paintings, wooden sculpture and Baroque art in 1979, Late Gothic winged altarpieces in 1982, and medieval and Renaissance stone carvings in 1985.

Beneath Building C lies the Habsburg Palatinal Crypt. Archduke Joseph, Palatine of Hungary from 1795 to 1847, was the first to convert the castle chapel crypts into a family burial place, and the marble sculpture of the palatine and the bronze angel are by György Zala. The crypt was broken into and ransacked in 1973 and then walled up; after restoration it was reconsecrated on 3 October 1987 and opened to the public in 1989. Twenty-four members of the family are now buried there. Visits are arranged by the museum, so look at its official page before planning to see it.
Good to know
The gallery is in Buda Castle; the castle hill can be reached on foot or by the funicular from Clark Ádám Square.
The same palace complex holds the Budapest History Museum in Building E and the National Széchényi Library in Building F.

Displays change, so check the official site before a visit built around the late medieval altarpieces: a tourism listing says they are to move to the Museum of Fine Arts after restoration, with no date given.
The Palatinal Crypt cannot be visited casually; the museum's official page explains how visits are arranged.

historyIntro: The Hungarian National Gallery preserves the long story of Hungarian visual art within the imposing buildings of Buda Castle.

historySections.heading: A national collection in the former palace

children.text: The Gallery took up its present accommodation in Buda Castle in 1975. The palace setting gives medieval religious works, nineteenth-century painting and newer art a striking historical framework.

The National Gallery and Museum of Fine Arts came under a unified institutional structure in 2012. Their collections tell complementary stories, with the Castle museum retaining its strong emphasis on Hungarian art.

name: Hungarian National Museum
description: Hungary's national museum occupies a Neoclassical building by Mihály Pollack, built between 1837 and 1847 and grown from Count Ferenc Széchényi's donation of 1802. The area in front of it is tied to the revolution of 15 March 1848, and its collections stretch from prehistory to the modern age, including the Medieval Hungarian Coronation Mantle.

children.text: The Hungarian National Museum is the country's main museum of history. It began on 25 November 1802, when Count Ferenc Széchényi decided to donate his collections to the nation; the gift included 11,884 printed volumes, 1,156 manuscripts, maps and engravings, thousands of gold coins and some antiquities and paintings. Act VIII of 1808 then formally established the museum. In 1813 the state bought the plot of the Batthyány family on which the present building stands, and Act XXXVII of 1836 funded a new building after János László Pyrker donated his picture gallery in 1836.

Mihály Pollack designed the Neoclassical building, which was constructed between 1837 and 1847 on Múzeum körút. Wikipedia names Raffael Monti of Milan as the maker of the statues in the portico, among them an allegorical figure of Hungary flanked by Science and Art. The staircase and ceiling were painted by Károly Lotz and Mór Than, whose work has been in place since 1875. The garden has hosted concerts, including performances by Ferenc Liszt.

The building holds a special place in Hungarian memory because of 15 March 1848. The square in front of the museum was one of the key sites of the revolution, and according to the museum, Sándor Petőfi addressed the crowd there; the museum adds that, contrary to later tradition, he did not recite the Nemzeti dal there, although popular tradition (repeated by Wikipedia) places its reading on the front steps. Ágoston Kubinyi, who directed the museum from 1843, was entrusted that morning by Petőfi and Jókai with two freshly printed leaflets, the Nemzeti dal and the Twelve Points, and in 1849 he obtained a safe-conduct for the museum from the imperial commander to protect its collections. The Ceremonial Hall hosted sessions of the Upper House of the first National Assembly in 1848, and the central state commemoration of the national holiday is held in front of the museum each year.

The permanent displays are arranged chronologically. Prehistory up to the Avar period, which ends in 804 AD, is on the ground floor, while the history of Hungary from 804 onwards is on the first floor, where the Medieval Hungarian Coronation Mantle is also kept. Medieval and early modern stone inscriptions are on the ground floor, and a Roman lapidary is in the basement. Objects mentioned in the museum's description include the 11th-century Byzantine enamel plaques of the Monomachus Crown, Scythian golden deer ornaments from the 6th century BC and the chainmail of the 15th-century commander Pál Kinizsi.

The museum once held far broader collections. A law of 1949 separated the ethnographic and natural-history collections, which became the Museum of Ethnography and the Hungarian Natural History Museum, and the National Széchényi Library became independent. The Castle Museum in Esztergom joined in 1985, and the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History became a department in 2017.
Good to know
The museum is at Múzeum körút 14–16 in District VIII.
The Metropolitan Ervin Szabó Library's Wenckheim Palace is a short walk from the museum, so the two can be visited together.
Exhibitions change, so check the museum's official site for current opening times, tickets and which displays are on view.
The museum's garden has long been used for concerts and festivals; check its programme for outdoor events.

heroImage.alt: The neoclassical portico of the Hungarian National Museum seen from its garden

historyIntro: The Hungarian National Museum is closely tied to the story of Hungarian national identity, cultural collecting and the revolutionary year of 1848.

historySections.heading: A home for the nation's collections

children.text: The museum originated in the nineteenth-century movement to preserve the country's historical and artistic heritage. Its monumental classical-style building and garden became a landmark in the changing urban landscape of Pest.

The area in front of the museum is strongly associated with the Hungarian Revolution of 1848 and public gatherings linked to its demands. The setting remains a place where museum collections and civic memory overlap.

name: City Park Boating Lake
description: The lake in front of Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park, where pedal boats, rowing boats and stand-up paddleboards are rented in the warmer months. In winter the same drained lakebed becomes the City Park Ice Rink, so the setting changes completely with the season.

children.text: The City Park lake lies in front of Vajdahunyad Castle, and the castle forms the backdrop for boaters. Visit Hungary notes that when the Rákos stream marshes were drained around the turn of the 18th and 19th centuries, an artificial lake with islands was created.

In summer it works as a boating lake. The lakeside operator rents pedal boats and, depending on the water level, rowboats and stand-up paddleboards in season, and the shore hosts summer events such as paddleboard yoga; check the operator for current boats and dates. The same announcement describes the water as a lake of 60,000 square metres, but the article does not say who operates it, so check the boating lake's own site for details.

In winter the lakebed is drained and the City Park Ice Rink takes its place. Wikipedia explains the cycle from the rink's side: in summer the rink area is flooded to form a pond used for boating. A guide to Budapest City Park similarly says that, depending on the season, visitors can skate or rent a rowing boat.
Good to know
Take the M1 metro to Széchenyi fürdő or Hősök tere; the lake is a short walk from either, or you can walk along Andrássy Avenue.
Confirm the operating season and what is available on the day on the boating lake's own site, since boats are seasonal.
The ice rink uses the same space in winter, so the lake looks very different from one month to the next.

historyIntro: The City Park lake shows how Budapest has long combined landscaped recreation with architecture and seasonal urban traditions.

historySections.heading: A lake beside historic park attractions

children.text: The water sits near Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park, surrounded by walking paths and landmark buildings associated with Budapest's late nineteenth-century development.

The lake's leisure uses have shifted with the weather: boating in warmer months and ice skating on its winter surface. The exact opening dates and operating arrangements belong to each season and should be confirmed with the operator.

name: City Park Ice Rink
description: A skating rink in City Park with a history going back to 1870, a neo-baroque main building and a surface of about 12,000 square metres. It has hosted European and world skating championships, and in warmer months the same space is flooded to form the boating lake.

children.text: The City Park rink grew out of the Skating Association of Pest, founded at the end of 1869 under Géza Kresz. According to Wikipedia the rink officially opened on 29 January 1870 in the presence of Rudolf, Crown Prince of Austria, and the first race was held on 2 February. On 6 January 1871 Jackson Haines gave a figure skating show there, and floodlights for night skating were installed in 1879.

The buildings changed as the rink grew. A wooden pavilion burned down in 1874 and was replaced by a skating hall designed by Ödön Lechner. The present neo-baroque main building, designed by Imre Francsek, followed in 1895 according to the rink's own history, Hungarian Wikipedia and Budapest heritage pages, although some sources give 1893. Championships followed: according to Hungarian Wikipedia the rink hosted the European Figure Skating Championships in 1895 and 1909 and world figure skating championships in 1929, 1935 and 1939.

Artificial ice was introduced on 26 November 1926, and the season grew to 105 days. Bombing in 1944 caused serious damage, though by autumn 1945 a larger part of the rink was serviceable again. In the 1960s the skating area was enlarged and standard 400-metre speed skating tracks were added.

A renovation between 2009 and 2011 gave the listed main building a full heritage restoration, and a 2011 business-press report says its entrance hall was returned to its original 1926 state, with gilded columns and railings. The rink reopened on 16 December 2011. Wikipedia gives the skating and bandy surface as 180 by 67 metres, the ice hockey rink as 60 by 30 metres and the total skating area as about 12,000 square metres. It describes the rink as the only bandy ice surface in Hungary. In summer the area is flooded to form a pond used for boating.
Good to know
Take the M1 metro to Széchenyi fürdő or Hősök tere; the rink is in the lakebed in front of Vajdahunyad Castle.
The rink operates on a separate seasonal calendar, so check the official site for current opening times, tickets and skate hire.
Skating can be combined with a walk to Heroes' Square and Andrássy Avenue.

historyIntro: The open-air rink is one of Budapest's classic winter traditions, turning the lake near Vajdahunyad Castle into a seasonal meeting place.

historySections.heading: Outdoor skating in the city park

children.text: The site's history is tied to the development of organised recreation in Városliget. The rink grew around the same park landscape whose historic buildings were reshaped by the millennium celebrations.

Skaters beneath the park's decorative architecture create one of Budapest's distinctive seasonal views. The rink is not a year-round attraction, and ice conditions, equipment rental and ticketing should always be checked for the actual visit.
